passage: Honestly, I was a bit of a copy machine last year. Tarun bhaiya was our senior in the debate club, and I thought he was flawless. I copied his haircut, his way of clearing his throat before speaking, even the phrases he used. My roommate said, "Who are you?" and I laughed it off. Then in one meeting Tarun bhaiya argued for something I disagreed with, and I clapped anyway, because that is what I did. Walking back, I realised I had not formed a thought of my own in months. It scared me a little. Now I still watch how he prepares and how patiently he listens, and I take that. But what I say in the debate hall, I decide. I am Nilesh again, and I like him better.

qa.q: What club was Tarun in when Nilesh admired him?
qa.a: Tarun was a senior in the debate club.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh feel scared after clapping for something he disagreed with?
qa.a: He realised he had not formed a thought of his own in months, and feared he was losing himself in copying someone else.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do to keep learning from seniors without copying?
qa.a: He can learn qualities like Tarun's preparation and patient listening, and test each opinion against his own judgement before he speaks or claps. 😊

qa.q: How might Nilesh's roommate have seen the copying?
qa.a: The roommate saw a friend becoming unfamiliar, hence "Who are you?", and may have been worried or puzzled. Nilesh laughed it off then, but it stayed in his mind.

grounding: A junior copies a senior's every move, then learns their qualities while keeping his own judgement.

passage:
'Irfan, why are you wearing a denim jacket? It's thirty-four degrees.'
'Baljeet-bhai wears one.'
'Baljeet-bhai is from Shimla. You're from Chennai.' His cousin Tanveer laughed and handed him water.
'He's the best debater in college. I want to be like him.'
'Fine. But you also switched from economics to philosophy because he did. You hate philosophy.'
'I don't hate it.'
'You fell asleep on the reading last night.'
Irfan tugged at the collar, sweating. 'He speaks so calmly. Everyone listens.'
'So learn that. Watch how he prepares. Ask him how he calms down before a debate. That's worth copying.'
'And the jacket?'
'The jacket is just sweat.'
Irfan took it off. 'Maybe I'll ask him on Friday how he prepares. And maybe I'll check if I can switch back to economics.'

qa.q: Which subject did Irfan switch to because Baljeet did?
qa.a: Irfan switched from economics to philosophy.

qa.q: What does Irfan feel toward Baljeet?
qa.a: Irfan feels admiration and a kind of longing, wishing he could speak as calmly as Baljeet and have everyone listen.

qa.q: What small step would help Irfan keep his own judgement?
qa.a: Learning Baljeet's real strengths, like how he prepares, while choosing his own subject, as Irfan plans to check about economics.

qa.q: How does Tanveer see Irfan's copying?
qa.a: Tanveer finds it funny but also worrying, watching Irfan lose himself in a jacket and a subject he does not enjoy.

grounding: Shows a junior copying a senior down to clothes and subject, and being nudged to learn the senior's qualities while keeping his own judgement.

passage: I'm Nazia, and last year I became a small copy of Yogesh without noticing. He was the final-year student who ran the college film society, and everything he said sounded right. I started using his phrases, 'visual grammar', 'honest frame', in reviews of films I hadn't even liked. I found slow black-and-white films dull, and suddenly I was praising three of them. When he called colour photography 'lazy', I stopped carrying my camera. It was my roommate who asked, 'When did you last shoot something?' I didn't have an answer. I still think Yogesh is brilliant; the way he listens before he speaks is something I really did learn. But this term I've gone back to shooting street colour, and at last week's screening I said I found the film boring. Yogesh just nodded.

qa.a: Yogesh ran the college film society.

qa.q: How does Nazia seem to feel looking back on the year of copying?
qa.a: Nazia seems a little embarrassed about it, but also relieved and proud to be shooting street colour again.

qa.q: What balance did Nazia find, and why does it work?
qa.a: Keeping a real quality learned from Yogesh, listening before speaking, while returning to Nazia's own taste and opinions.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Nazia's honest opinion at the screening?
qa.a: Yogesh seems to take it calmly with a nod, suggesting honest disagreement was always welcome.

grounding: A first-person look back at copying a senior's every opinion, and at keeping his good qualities while recovering one's own judgement.
